title: India's Russian Oil Imports Hit Record 2.8 Million Barrels Per Day in July
excerpt: Indian refiners purchased a record volume of Russian crude in July for the second straight month, even as the U.S. sanctions waiver expired and the Trump administration weighed tariffs of up to 100% on major Russian oil buyers.
body:
• India imported a record 2.8 million barrels per day of Russian crude in July 2026, making up 55.5% of the country's total crude imports
  • Russian crude shipments to India were worth €5.5 billion in July — a 2.1% volume increase over June's previous record — with smaller ports driving the surge
  • Indian refineries continue exporting refined petroleum products worth hundreds of millions of euros to countries that have sanctioned Moscow, including the EU and the United States

A New Monthly Record

India's crude oil purchases from Russia reached an all-time high of 2.8 million barrels per day (bpd) in July 2026, according to data compiled by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). The figure represents roughly 55.5% of India's total crude imports of just over 5 million bpd — and marks the second consecutive month in which Russian crude imports set a record.

In value terms, India imported Russian crude worth €5.5 billion during July, with crude oil accounting for 87% of the country's total Russian fossil fuel purchases of €6.4 billion. Coal (€512 million) and refined oil products (€341 million) made up the remainder.

The trajectory has been steep. Russia supplied fewer than 100,000 bpd of crude to India in 2021, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration — roughly 2.5% of Indian imports. That jumped to about 740,000 bpd in 2022 after Western sanctions prompted Moscow to offer deep discounts, climbed to 1.8 million bpd in 2023, and averaged about the same in 2024 before surging past 2 million bpd in early 2026.

Smaller Ports Drove the Surge

The July record was driven by higher volumes at India's smaller refining terminals rather than its two largest ports. Imports at HMEL's Mundra terminal jumped 58% from June, deliveries at Indian Oil's Vadinar SMPL terminal rose 35%, and Russian crude arrivals at Mumbai increased 37%.

Volumes at Jamnagar — one of the world's largest refining complexes, operated by Reliance Industries — remained flat, and Paradip saw a 22% decline. The record was achieved entirely on the strength of increased receipts at other facilities, according to CREA.

"India was the second-largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels in July 2026, importing a total of 6.4 billion euros worth of Russian hydrocarbons."

— Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA)

Urals Pricing and the Price Cap

The average price of Russia's Urals crude declined 3% in July to $60.22 per barrel, according to CREA — still well above the G7 and EU price cap of $44.10 per barrel that took effect in February 2026. Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, India has become the second-largest purchaser of Russian crude globally, accounting for 37% of Russia's crude exports. China remained the largest buyer with a 50% share.

Refined Products Flowing to Sanctioning Nations

India's role extends beyond importing crude. Indian refineries processing Russian oil continue to export refined petroleum products to countries that have sanctioned Moscow.

Refineries in India, Turkiye, Brunei, and Georgia that processed Russian crude exported refined products worth a combined €633 million to sanctioning countries in July, according to CREA. Of that, €234 million went to the United States, €214 million to the European Union, and €184 million to Australia. Five cargoes from Indian refineries were discharged at EU ports despite the bloc's ban on Russian-origin refined products, which took effect on January 21.

The United States also received refined products from Reliance's Jamnagar refinery, where Russian crude accounted for about 35% of feedstock over the three months ending in July.

What's Next: Tariff Threats and Diplomatic Pressure

The record imports arrive at a politically fraught moment. The U.S. sanctions waiver on Russian crude has expired, and the Trump administration is pushing a sanctions bill that would authorize tariffs of up to 100% on the largest importers of Russian oil — a provision aimed squarely at India and China.

India has resisted Western pressure, framing its purchases as a matter of energy security for a nation that imports more than 85% of its oil needs. For global energy markets, India's sustained buying means Russian crude continues to find ready buyers regardless of Western sanctions. Whether triple-digit tariff threats change that calculus remains the key variable for the second half of 2026.
nri_angle: India's record Russian oil imports carry direct implications for global energy prices and US-India trade relations, with the Trump administration threatening tariffs that could affect Indian refiners and the broader diaspora economy.
